implementation_notes: C++23 ships the pattern as std::expected<T, E>: exactly one of the value or a std::unexpected<E> is stored, the object is never valueless, and and_then/transform/or_else/transform_error chain fallible steps without nesting conditionals. Before C++23 the same interface exists as the single-header tl::expected (C++11), and a plain std::variant<T, E> with std::visit is the standard-library fallback when a third-party header is not acceptable. std::expected is the default because it makes the failure branch explicit while keeping the success path linear; keep std::variant for outcomes where neither branch is an error.
pitfalls: expected is never valueless, but value() on an error branch throws std::bad_expected_access: the checked accessor is the C++ unwrap and belongs in tests, not in the request path.
T cannot be a reference, an array or void (nor can E), and both types must be Destructible objects, so reference results need std::reference_wrapper and void results need the void specialization.
std::variant tolerates the same type more than once, so a variant<T, T> compiles but get<T> can no longer discriminate the alternative - use distinct reason types or std::expected instead.

variants.name: std::variant plus std::visit
variants.implementation_notes: C++17's type-safe union gives the same two-case structure without an error-specific API: one alternative holds the value, the other the reason, and std::visit (or index() together with get_if) performs the case analysis. Prefer it when both branches are legitimate outcomes rather than value-versus-error, or when the toolchain has to stay on C++17; the monadic helpers are yours to write, and an overload set is the usual way to keep the visitor readable.
pitfalls: A variant can become valueless only when an exception escapes during assignment, but std::visit then throws std::bad_variant_access: do not assume index() stays in range after a throwing move.
A template catch-all overload in the visitor compiles for every alternative and silently swallows the ones you forgot; one overload per alternative is what makes a new case a compile error.
Default construction selects alternative 0, so put the value first or use std::monostate, otherwise a default-constructed outcome claims to be an error.

variants.name: tl::expected backport
variants.implementation_notes: tl::expected is a single-header implementation of the same interface for C++11/14/17 projects: and_then, map, map_error and or_else are available today, and the type is written to be replaced by std::expected once the toolchain moves to C++23. Choose it when the language floor cannot be raised but the code should still read like the C++23 version; the cost is a vendored third-party header whose type name appears in every signature.
pitfalls: Misuse is checked with TL_ASSERT (a plain assert by default) rather than exceptions, so calling .error() on a value or dereferencing an error aborts in debug builds and is undefined behaviour in release builds.
The header defines tl::expected, not std::expected: migrating later is a mechanical rename, and mixing both types in one interface creates two incompatible error contracts.
